summary.text: 上 means “above” or “up”; its early graph is interpreted as a positional mark above a reference line. The early line is described as curved in some accounts and horizontal in others.

formation.text: 上 is an indicative graph, not a compound of semantic or phonetic components. Its early construction is interpreted as a short mark above a reference line to indicate the upper position; sources differ on whether some early lines were curved or horizontal. This historical analysis describes the earlier construction, not a decomposition of the present strokes. The received Shuowen text also classifies 上 as indicative, a Han-era analysis rather than independent confirmation of the earlier history.

history.text: Early forms are described as a short mark above a longer reference line, though accounts differ on whether the line was curved or horizontal. Later forms altered the upper mark, with Spring-and-Autumn forms adding a vertical stroke to distinguish 上 from 二; the modern standard form has a dot above a horizontal stroke. These are graphic changes, not evidence of a change in meaning.

The received Shuowen text treats 丄 as an ancient form meaning “high” and 上 as its seal-script form. Received editions differ over whether the head form is 丄 or 二; this is a difference in the transmitted lexicographic tradition, not confirmation of Shang graphic history.

uncertainties.text: The earliest graph form discussed is oracle-bone 上, but no earlier dated occurrence is established. Paleographic accounts report inscriptional examples; a photograph of an artifact transcribed with 上甲 does not isolate that character.
Accounts agree on a mark above a reference line but differ on whether the early line was curved or horizontal; no primary inscription image resolves this variation.

Reported uses include spatial “above/upper side” and “at/on the side of,” authority-related meanings, and verbs glossed “ascend” and “send up.” The evidence does not establish a dated sequence or semantic connections among these uses. The reported 以上 meaning “more than” is a compound use, not evidence for a single-character sense.

senses.period: Zhou bronze inscription contexts reported; current use
senses.text: Reported Shang-period examples include 上帝, 上甲, and contrasts with 下; Zhou bronze examples include spatial ‘above.’ The cited dictionary definitions also support ‘above; upper side’ as a current meaning, without establishing priority among every lexical use.
Bronze-inscription accounts report this spatial use. Its relationship to “above” is not established.
Current dictionary definitions include rank-related “superior”; the reported historical uses do not establish its sequence relative to spatial “above.”

limitations.text: Early spatial uses are supported, and several other uses are reported, but dated semantic transitions among them are not established. 上帝 and 上甲 are compound examples, not automatically independent senses of 上.

The reported 以上 example means “more than” in a compound and does not establish a single-character sense. Supplied reconstructed phonological rows separately gloss 上 as “ascend,” “put up,” and “top, above”; these rows do not establish attested usage, semantic chronology, or graphic origin.

overview.text: 上 commonly means “above” or “upper.” Its early graph is interpreted as a mark above a reference line; accounts differ on whether that line was curved or horizontal.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; modern vector rendering, not a dated artifact
items.caption: This seal-script-style rendering has a long horizontal baseline, a central upright, and an upper stroke that bends right and descends into the upright. It shows a received seal-style form of 上; the image does not date its relation to earlier forms.
items.alt: A black glyph with a long horizontal baseline, a central upright, and an upper stroke that bends right and descends into it.
items.selection_reason: It provides a clear example of the received seal-script-style form, complementing accounts of early 上 as a mark above a reference line. The modern redraw does not establish a dated transition between those forms.
